title: Social Media Feed
summary: Show each user a fast, ranked home feed of posts from the accounts they follow, including accounts with tens of millions of followers.
problem: Design the home feed of a social network. Users publish posts (text with optional images or video), follow other users, and open a home feed with recent and relevant posts from the accounts they follow. The feed must load quickly and scroll without gaps or duplicates, even when a follower count ranges from ten to fifty million.
functional: Create a post; follow and unfollow users
Home feed: posts from followed accounts, newest first at minimum, with an optional ranking step
Cursor-based infinite scroll through the feed with no duplicates when new posts arrive
Like and comment counts shown on each post
A user profile page lists that user's own posts
nonFunctional: Feed read latency under 200 ms at the 99th percentile
A new post reaches followers within a few seconds for normal accounts (eventual consistency is acceptable)
Highly available; a stale feed is better than an error
Handles the skew: most users have hundreds of followers, a few have tens of millions
constraints: 100 million daily active users, about 20 million new posts per day
Each active user opens the feed about 10 times a day
Average follow count about 200; a long tail of celebrity accounts
Images and video go through an existing media service and CDN; you only store references
deliverables: Requirements and the assumptions you made
A capacity estimate: posts per second, feed reads per second, fan-out writes per second, and feed cache size
A high-level architecture diagram (Mermaid or an uploaded image)
The API (endpoints, pagination parameters, payloads) and the data model
Your fan-out strategy and how you handle celebrity accounts
How ranking, caching and pagination work
How it scales, how it fails, and what you would monitor
The main trade-offs and what you chose not to build
hints: Work out the number of feed writes per second if every post is pushed to every follower. Then work out what one celebrity post costs.
Fan-out on write makes reads cheap and writes expensive; fan-out on read is the opposite. A mix may beat either.
Offset pagination breaks on a feed that changes while it is read. What can you use instead?
A feed does not need to store posts, only post ids in order.
reference:
This is one reasonable design. The numbers are estimates to show the reasoning; adjust them and the conclusions follow.

### Capacity estimate
- Posts: 20 million per day / 86,400 s is about 230 posts/s on average. Assume peak is 3x, so about 700/s.
- Feed reads: 100 million users x 10 opens per day = 1 billion/day, about 12,000/s on average and 35,000/s at peak. The read:write ratio is roughly 50:1, so reads must be cheap.
- Fan-out on write for normal accounts: 230 posts/s x 200 followers is about 46,000 feed-entry writes/s on average, about 140,000/s at peak. That is high but fine for a sharded in-memory store fed by a queue.
- One celebrity post with 30 million followers would be 30 million writes in one burst. That one number is why pure push fails.
- Feed cache: store about 500 entries per active user, each a post id (8 bytes) and a score or timestamp (8 bytes), about 16 bytes: 500 x 16 B = 8 KB per user. For 100 million users that is about 800 GB, so a Redis (or similar) cluster of some tens of nodes with replicas.
- Post storage: 20 million posts/day x about 1 KB of metadata is about 20 GB/day, about 7 TB/year. Media is separate, in object storage behind a CDN.

### Architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> GW[API gateway]
  GW --> PS[Post service]
  GW --> FS[Feed service]
  GW --> GS[Graph service: follows]
  PS --> PDB[(Post store, sharded by post id)]
  PS --> Q[[Fan-out queue]]
  Q --> FW[Fan-out workers]
  FW --> GS
  FW --> FC[(Feed cache: sorted list per user)]
  FS --> FC
  FS --> PC[(Post cache)]
  PC --> PDB
  FS --> CP[(Celebrity post lists)]
  FS --> RK[Ranking service]
  PS --> CP
```

**Write path.** The client posts to the post service. It stores the post (id from a time-ordered generator such as a Snowflake-style id, so ids sort by time), then publishes a small event to a queue and returns. Fan-out workers read the event, fetch the author's follower list from the graph service, and for each follower push the post id into that follower's feed list in the cache. Workers only push to followers who were active recently; inactive users get their feed rebuilt when they return.

**Celebrity problem (hybrid).** If an author has more than a threshold of followers (say 100,000), the post is not fanned out. It is only written to the author's own post list. When a user opens their feed, the feed service reads the precomputed feed (pushed posts from normal accounts) and merges in recent posts from the few celebrities that user follows (pulled at read time, from a cached list per celebrity). A user follows only a handful of celebrities, so the merge is cheap and the celebrity list is one of the hottest cache keys, which caches well.

**Read path.** The feed service reads the first page of ids from the user's feed list, merges celebrity posts, optionally calls ranking, then hydrates ids into full posts using a post cache (batch get; misses go to the post store), and adds counts and the author's profile data from their own caches. Hydration at read time means edits and deletes show up immediately and the feed list stays tiny.

### API
- `POST /v1/posts` body `{ "text": "...", "mediaIds": ["m1"] }` returns `201` with the post.
- `GET /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=<opaque>` returns `{ "items": [...], "nextCursor": "..." }`.
- `GET /v1/users/{id}/posts?limit=20&cursor=...`
- `PUT /v1/users/{id}/follow` and `DELETE /v1/users/{id}/follow`.

**Pagination.** Use a cursor, not an offset. The cursor encodes the position, for example the (score, post id) of the last item returned. With offset, a new post pushed to the top shifts everything and the next page repeats an item. A cursor says "items older than this", so new posts do not disturb it. If ranking reorders items, snapshot the ranked candidate list for the session (or cache it for a short time keyed by a feed session id) so scrolling stays consistent.

### Data model
- `posts`: post_id (time-ordered), author_id, text, media refs, created_at. Sharded by post id (or by author id if you favour profile page locality; that creates hot shards for celebrities, so many teams shard by post id and keep a separate author index).
- `follows`: (follower_id, followee_id, created_at), stored twice, indexed by follower and by followee, in a store sharded by the indexed user, because you need both "who do I follow" and "who follows me".
- `feed:{user_id}`: a sorted collection of (post_id, score), capped to about 500 entries by trimming the oldest.
- `counters`: likes and comments counts, updated asynchronously and cached, since exact real-time counts are not required.

### Ranking
Start with reverse chronological: it is predictable, cheap and easy to explain. When ranking is added, do it in two stages: candidate generation (the merged feed list, a few hundred ids) and then a scoring step using features such as author affinity, post age, engagement so far, and media type, producing a score by a model or weighted formula. Keep the model behind the ranking service interface with a timeout and fall back to chronological order if it is slow or down.

### Scaling and failure handling
- The queue absorbs bursts; workers scale horizontally by partitioning on follower shard. Retries must be idempotent: adding the same post id to a sorted set twice changes nothing.
- Feed cache loss: rebuild a user's feed on demand from the graph and the recent post lists (the pull path), which is the same code used for inactive users, so the fallback is exercised daily.
- Hot keys: a celebrity's post list and a viral post are read by millions. Replicate those keys, add a short local in-process cache in the feed service, and let CDN or edge caching serve the post media.
- Fan-out lag: if the queue backs up, feeds get fresher posts later but still load. Monitor queue age, not just depth.
- Deleted posts and blocked users: filter at hydration time, so no one has to scrub millions of lists.
- Monitor: feed p50/p99 latency, cache hit rate, fan-out queue age, post-to-visible delay, hydration miss rate, ranking timeout rate.

### Trade-offs and alternatives
- **Push vs pull vs hybrid.** Pure pull is simple and exact but makes each read do a heavy merge across hundreds of accounts. Pure push makes reads fast but multiplies writes and fails on celebrities. The hybrid costs more code and a threshold to tune, in return for both fast reads and bounded writes. The threshold is a tunable, not a law.
- **Store the feed as ids, not copies of posts.** Storage is tiny and edits are consistent, but each read pays for hydration. Storing full posts in the feed would remove that cost and make every edit a massive rewrite.
- **Cache only active users.** Saves memory but a returning user's first load is slower. Another option is a longer retention for more users at a higher cost.
- **Eventual consistency.** A user may not see their own post at once in their own feed unless you insert it into their own list synchronously (cheap and worth doing).
- **Not built here:** ads insertion, stories, spam and abuse filtering, real-time push of new posts to open feeds (a websocket or "new posts" banner), and a full recommendation system for posts from accounts the user does not follow.
